Step 1 — The elastic sector and where T comes from

For small transverse displacements of an already pre-stressed sheet, the effective elastic Lagrangian density is
\boxed{\;\mathcal L_u=\frac{\rho}{2}\,\dot X^2-\frac{T}{2}\,|\nabla X|^2\;}
\tag{1}
in local inertial coordinates (flat background, slow motion). Here:
	•	X(\mathbf r,t) is the transverse displacement field on the sheet.
	•	\rho is the surface mass density (kg·m^{-2}).
	•	T is the pre-tension (N·m^{-1}), i.e., the uniform in-plane stress set by boundary stretch/clamping.
	•	In the full SAT/Blockwave picture, T is an emergent parameter: it is the background value of in-plane stress that minimizes the static part of \mathcal L_u for the chosen boundary conditions (a fixed rim sets the pre-strain; linearizing about that background yields the quadratic form (1)). For Chapter 1 we treat T as fixed by the setup, exactly as in standard membrane theory.

Varying (1) gives the membrane wave equation:
\boxed{\;\rho\,\ddot X=T\,\nabla^2 X\;}
\tag{2}
the textbook drumhead/trampoline dynamics.

Step 2 — Mode spectrum on a circular bed (explicit)

On a disk of radius R with clamped rim X(R,\phi,t)=0, the eigenmodes are
X_{mn}(r,\phi,t)=\Re\!\left\{\psi_{mn}(r,\phi)\,e^{i\omega_{mn} t}\right\},
\qquad
\psi_{mn}(r,\phi)=J_m\!\Big(\tfrac{\alpha_{mn} r}{R}\Big)\,e^{im\phi},
where \alpha_{mn} is the n-th positive zero of J_m. The dispersion from (2) is
\boxed{\;\omega_{mn}=\frac{\alpha_{mn}}{R}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\rho}}\;}
\tag{3}
The fundamental mode is m=0,n=1: \alpha_{01}\approx 2.404825557, so
\omega_0=\frac{\alpha_{01}}{R}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\rho}}.
\tag{4}

Step 3 — From field to single-DOF spring (derive k_{\rm eff})

Let the generalized coordinate be the center displacement q(t)\equiv X(0,t). For the fundamental mode,
X(r,t)=q(t)\,\psi_0(r),\quad \psi_0(r)=\frac{J_0(\alpha_{01} r/R)}{J_0(0)}=J_0\!\Big(\tfrac{\alpha_{01} r}{R}\Big),
\quad \psi_0(0)=1.
Insert this ansatz into the quadratic energy from (1):
E=\frac{1}{2}\rho\int_{\!A}\dot X^2\,dA+\frac{1}{2}T\int_{\!A}|\nabla X|^2\,dA
=\frac{1}{2}M_{\rm eff}\,\dot q^2+\frac{1}{2}K_{\rm eff}\,q^2.
The effective modal mass is
M_{\rm eff}=\rho\int_A \psi_0^2\,dA
=\rho\,2\pi\!\int_0^{R}\!r\,J_0^2(\alpha_{01} r/R)\,dr
=\rho\,\pi R^2\,J_1^2(\alpha_{01}),
\tag{5}
using the identity \int_0^1 x\,J_0^2(\alpha x)\,dx=\tfrac12\!\big[J_0^2(\alpha)+J_1^2(\alpha)\big] and J_0(\alpha_{01})=0. Numerically J_1(\alpha_{01})\approx 0.519147, so
M_{\rm eff}\;\approx\;0.2695\,\rho\,\pi R^2.
The effective modal stiffness follows either from the gradient integral or simply via K_{\rm eff}=M_{\rm eff}\,\omega_0^2:
K_{\rm eff}=M_{\rm eff}\,\omega_0^2
=\Big(\rho\,\pi R^2 J_1^2(\alpha_{01})\Big)\,\Big(\frac{\alpha_{01}^2}{R^2}\frac{T}{\rho}\Big)
=\boxed{\;C_0\,T\;},\quad
C_0\equiv \pi\,\alpha_{01}^2\,J_1^2(\alpha_{01})\approx 4.90.
\tag{6}
So, for the center coordinate normalized as q=X(0), the membrane behaves—near the fundamental mode—like a linear spring with stiffness \sim 4.90\,T. (Order-unity constants change with your choice of coordinate/normalization; the key point is: stiffness \propto T with no hidden dependence when the mode is normalized at the center. For static point indentation one instead finds K\simeq 4\pi T/\ln(8R/a) with contact radius a; both are consistent in their respective limits.)

Coupling a point mass m at the center to the modal coordinate gives the single-DOF equation
m\,\ddot q + K_{\rm eff}\,q = 0, \qquad
\boxed{\;q(t)=A\cos(\omega t+\phi),\quad \omega=\sqrt{\frac{K_{\rm eff}}{m}}=\sqrt{\frac{C_0\,T}{m}}\;}
\tag{7}
and the bounce period T_{\rm bounce}=2\pi/\omega.

Step 4 — Energy exchange at the bottom (explicit)

At small amplitude with negligible damping, gravitational potential converts to elastic energy:
\boxed{\;m g h=\tfrac12 K_{\rm eff}\,q_{\max}^2=\tfrac12\,C_0\,T\,q_{\max}^2\;}
\tag{8}
which fixes the maximum deflection q_{\max} reached from a release height h.

Step 5 — Second, unrelated domain (gravity) from the same action

Independently, the Einstein–Hilbert term in \mathcal L yields, in the Newtonian limit,
\nabla^2\Phi=4\pi G\rho_{\rm mass},\qquad \Phi\simeq gz\ \text{near Earth’s surface},
recovering the same mg that appears in (8). Two unrelated sectors—membrane elasticity and Newtonian gravity—arrive from one action, without importing extra assumptions in this chapter. (Again: \mathcal L_J and F(\theta) remain dormant here.)

\section*{Promise of the Chapter}
Up to now, we have been sampling. One track at a time: elasticity, gravity, scalars, quantized flux, spectra.  
Each sounded clean enough on its own. But a kernel is only real if it can play them all at once.  
This chapter shows, carefully and without flourish, how the same SAT/Blockwave action produces multiple familiar sectors together, and how the integers of the 3-form current enter all of them.  

\section{The Kernel on Display}
We begin from the full action in its four-dimensional form:
\begin{align}
\mathcal L &= \frac{M_P^2}{2} R + \frac{f_\theta}{2}(\partial\theta)^2 - \Lambda_\theta^4 (1-\cos\theta) \\
&\quad + \mathcal L_u[g,u,X] + \mathcal L_J[g,u,J] + \frac{g_h}{2} F(\theta)\, J_{\mu\nu\rho}J^{\mu\nu\rho}.
\end{align}

Declared fields:
\begin{itemize}
  \item $g_{\mu\nu}$: metric, with $R$ the scalar curvature.
  \item $u^\mu$: time-flow field, constrained by $u^\mu u_\mu=-1$.
  \item $\theta$: compact scalar, periodic $\theta\sim\theta+2\pi$.
  \item $J_{\mu\nu\rho}$: conserved three-form current; dual $\tilde J^\mu = \tfrac{1}{3!}\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}J_{\nu\rho\sigma}$ with $\nabla_\mu \tilde J^\mu=0$.
\end{itemize}

All of these have already appeared in isolation. Here they sit side by side, unedited.  

\section{Background and Perturbations}
We expand around flat space:
\[
g_{\mu\nu}=\eta_{\mu\nu}+h_{\mu\nu},\qquad |h_{\mu\nu}|\ll 1,
\]
with $u^\mu=(1,0,0,0)+\delta u^\mu$, small perturbations to the time-flow, and
\[
J_{\mu\nu\rho}= \bar J_{\mu\nu\rho}+\delta J_{\mu\nu\rho},\qquad \theta=\bar\theta+\varphi,
\]
where bars denote backgrounds, $\varphi$ a fluctuation.

The background three-form is chosen constant:
\[
\bar J_{123} = n,\qquad \text{all others zero}.
\]
This integer $n$ is the conserved flux sector.

\section{Variation and Equations of Motion}
Varying the action to quadratic order in fluctuations gives three coupled equations:

\paragraph{(i) Gravity sector.} From the Einstein--Hilbert term,
\[
\Box \bar h_{\mu\nu} - \partial_\mu \partial^\rho \bar h_{\rho\nu} - \partial_\nu \partial^\rho \bar h_{\rho\mu}
+ \partial_\mu \partial_\nu \bar h - \eta_{\mu\nu}(\Box \bar h - \partial^\rho\partial^\sigma \bar h_{\rho\sigma})= -\frac{1}{M_P^2}\,T_{\mu\nu}.
\]
Linearized Einstein equation, as in Chapter 2.

\paragraph{(ii) Scalar sector.} Expanding the potential gives
\[
V(\varphi) = \frac{1}{2}\frac{\Lambda_\theta^4}{f_\theta}\,\varphi^2 - \frac{1}{4!}\frac{\Lambda_\theta^4}{f_\theta^2}\,\varphi^4 + \cdots,
\]
so $\varphi$ is a scalar of mass $m_\varphi^2=\Lambda_\theta^4/f_\theta$ with self-coupling $\lambda=\Lambda_\theta^4/f_\theta^2$, as in Chapter 3.

\paragraph{(iii) Three-form sector.} The coupling term gives
\[
\mathcal L_{J\theta} = \frac{g_h}{2}\,F(\bar\theta)\, \delta J_{\mu\nu\rho}\delta J^{\mu\nu\rho}
+ g_h F'(\bar\theta)\,\varphi\,\bar J_{\mu\nu\rho}\delta J^{\mu\nu\rho}+\cdots.
\]
The first term is a quadratic kinetic for $\delta J$, the second couples it to the scalar fluctuation.

\section{The Anchor Derivation: One Action, Two Operators}
Here is the Bessel-equivalent demonstration: that the same kernel yields both Einstein gravity and a gauge-like sector, coupled through the 3-form integer $n$.

1.\; Fix Lorentz gauge for gravity: $\partial^\mu \bar h_{\mu\nu}=\tfrac12\partial_\nu \bar h$.  
This reduces the linearized Einstein equation to
\[
\Box \bar h_{\mu\nu} = -\frac{1}{M_P^2} T_{\mu\nu}.
\]

2.\; For the 3-form, take the dual vector $\tilde J^\mu$. Conservation $\nabla_\mu \tilde J^\mu=0$ makes $\tilde J^\mu$ behave like a gauge current. Its quadratic action after dualization is
\[
\mathcal L_{\tilde J} = -\frac{1}{4g_{\rm eff}^2} F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu},\qquad F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu \tilde J_\nu - \partial_\nu \tilde J_\mu,
\]
with $g_{\rm eff}^{-2}\sim g_h F(\bar\theta)\,n^2$.

3.\; The scalar couples to both through $F'(\bar\theta)$, shifting its mass by an $n$-dependent term:
\[
m_{\rm eff}^2 = \frac{\Lambda_\theta^4}{f_\theta} + \frac{g_h n^2}{f_\theta}.
\]

Thus, from one action:  
- Linearized gravity (Einstein operator).  
- A Maxwell-like gauge sector from the 3-form dual.  
- A scalar whose mass depends on the same integer $n$.

This is not hand-waving: the operators appear explicitly side by side.

\section*{Math spine: “So You Want to Watch One Evaporate?”}

\subsection*{1. Hawking temperature from surface gravity}
For Schwarzschild,
\[
ds^2=-\Big(1-\frac{2M}{r}\Big)dt^2+\Big(1-\frac{2M}{r}\Big)^{-1}dr^2+r^2 d\Omega^2,
\quad r_h=2M.
\]
Surface gravity \(\kappa\) is
\[
\kappa=\frac{1}{2}\,\partial_r g_{tt}\Big|_{r=r_h}=\frac{1}{4M}.
\]
Hawking’s relation \(T_H=\kappa/(2\pi)\) gives
\[
T_H=\frac{1}{8\pi M}.
\]
% (Hawking 1974, 1975)

\subsection*{2. Radiated power scaling}
Blackbody estimate (ignoring graybody factors): \(P\sim A\,\sigma T_H^4\) with area \(A=4\pi r_h^2=16\pi M^2\).
Thus
\[
P \sim 16\pi M^2 \times \sigma \Big(\frac{1}{8\pi M}\Big)^4
= \frac{\sigma}{(8\pi)^4}\,\frac{16\pi}{M^2}
\;\propto\; \frac{1}{M^2}.
\]
Restoring the frequency-dependent transmission (graybody) factors just renormalizes the prefactor \(\alpha\) below (Page 1976).

\subsection*{3. Mass-loss ODE and solution}
Energy conservation: \(\dot M=-P\Rightarrow \dot M\sim -\alpha/M^2\) for some constant \(\alpha>0\).
Integrate:
\[
\int_{M_0}^{M(t)} M^2\,dM = -\alpha\!\int_0^t dt' 
\;\Rightarrow\;
\frac{M(t)^3-M_0^3}{3}=-\alpha t,
\quad
M(t)=\big(M_0^3-3\alpha t\big)^{1/3}.
\]

\subsection*{4. Area quantization and rung size}
Assume uniformly spaced horizon area eigenvalues
\[
A=n\,\Delta A,\qquad n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}.
\]
First law \(dM=\frac{\kappa}{8\pi}\,dA\) implies a discrete step “energy”
\[
\Delta M \equiv \mathcal E_1=\frac{\kappa}{8\pi}\,\Delta A.
\]
For Schwarzschild \(\kappa=1/(4M)\):
\[
\boxed{\;\mathcal E_1(M)=\frac{\Delta A}{32\pi\,M}\;}
\]
Two common choices:
\[
\Delta A_{\text{Bek}}=8\pi \ell_P^2
\;\Rightarrow\;
\mathcal E_1=\frac{\ell_P^2}{4M},
\qquad
\Delta A_{\text{Hod/Muk}}=4\ln 3\,\ell_P^2
\;\Rightarrow\;
\mathcal E_1=\frac{\ln 3}{8\pi}\frac{\ell_P^2}{M}.
\]

\subsection*{5. Flux difference equation (SAT ladder)}
In SAT, area rungs come from flux integers \(n\rightarrow n-1\). Identifying one rung emission with one quantum of energy \(\mathcal E_1\) yields
\[
M_{n}-M_{n-1}=\mathcal E_1(M_{n})=\frac{\Delta A}{32\pi\,M_n}.
\]
\emph{Dimensions check (SI):} with \(\Delta A\) in m\(^2\), \(\kappa=c^4/(4GM)\), 
\(
\mathcal E_1=\kappa\,\Delta A/(8\pi)
= \frac{c^4}{4GM}\frac{\Delta A}{8\pi}
\) has units J, as required.

\subsection*{6. Continuum limit (ladder \(\to\) ODE)}
Write \(A=16\pi M^2=n\Delta A\Rightarrow n=\frac{16\pi M^2}{\Delta A}\).
A step \(n\to n-1\) changes mass by \(\Delta M=\mathcal E_1(M)\).
With step time \(\tau_{\rm step}\), the finite difference
\[
\frac{M_{n}-M_{n-1}}{\tau_{\rm step}}
\;\to\;
\frac{dM}{dt}
\quad\text{as}\quad \Delta A\to 0,
\]
and using \(\mathcal E_1\propto 1/M\) one recovers \(\dot M\propto -1/M^2\) after integrating over the blackbody spectrum (the prefactor matches the Hawking/Page \(\alpha\) once graybody factors are included). Thus Hawking’s smooth fade is the \(\Delta A\!\to\!0\) limit of the SAT staircase.

\subsection*{7. Entropy step and emission probability}
Bekenstein–Hawking entropy \(S=A/4\) gives a per-rung entropy change
\[
\boxed{\;\Delta S=\frac{\Delta A}{4}\;}
\]
so the Boltzmann-like weight for a single step scales as
\[
\Gamma_{n\to n-1}\;\propto\; e^{-\Delta S}=e^{-\Delta A/4}.
\]
For \(\Delta A=4\ln k\,\ell_P^2\), one finds \(\Delta S=\ln k\) and evenly spaced line intensities by a factor \(k^{-1}\) per rung (Bekenstein–Mukhanov 1995).

\subsection*{8. Line (comb) spectrum and thermal limit}
A single rung drop releases energy \(\Delta E=\mathcal E_1\). The fundamental angular frequency spacing is
\[
\Delta\omega=\frac{\Delta E}{\hbar}.
\]
In SI, with \(\Delta A=8\pi\ell_P^2\), one gets
\[
\Delta E=\frac{\hbar c}{4M},
\quad
\Delta f=\frac{\Delta E}{h}=\frac{c}{8\pi M}.
\]
With \(\Delta A=4\ln 3\,\ell_P^2\),
\(
\Delta f=\frac{c\ln 3}{16\pi^2 M}.
\)
As \(M\) grows, \(\Delta f\to 0\) and closely spaced lines merge into a thermal continuum; as \(M\) shrinks late in evaporation, spacing widens and discreteness can imprint a comb-like modulation.

\subsection*{9. Numbers (order-of-magnitude, SI)}
Planck area \(\ell_P^2\simeq 2.612\times 10^{-70}{\rm~m}^2\).
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Solar mass} \(M_\odot=1.9885\times10^{30}{\rm~kg}\).
\[
\Delta A_{\text{Bek}}=8\pi\ell_P^2\simeq 6.57\times10^{-69}{\rm~m}^2,
\quad
\Delta f_{\text{Bek}}=\frac{c}{8\pi M_\odot}\approx 6.0\times 10^{-24}{\rm~Hz}.
\]
Hod/Mukhanov spacing:
\(\Delta f \approx \dfrac{c\ln 3}{16\pi^2 M_\odot}\approx 1.05\times10^{-24}{\rm~Hz}\).
(Effectively unobservable: periods \(\gtrsim 10^{16}\) years.)

\item \textbf{Primordial BH} \(M=10^{12}{\rm~kg}\).
\[
\Delta f_{\text{Bek}}\approx \frac{c}{8\pi M}\approx 1.19\times10^{-5}{\rm~Hz}\quad(\text{period }\sim\! 1~\text{day}),
\]
\[
\Delta f_{\text{Hod/Muk}}\approx 2.09\times10^{-6}{\rm~Hz}.
\]
Still tiny, but late-time steps for even smaller \(M\) move into Hz–kHz as \(M\to 10^{7}\!-\!10^{4}{\rm~kg}\):
\[
\Delta f_{\text{Bek}}\approx
\begin{cases}
\;1.19~{\rm Hz} & (M=10^{7}{\rm~kg}),\\
\;1.19~{\rm kHz} & (M=10^{4}{\rm~kg}).
\end{cases}
\]
Such BHs are ultra-short-lived; this scaling just shows the trend.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Mini-summary (for the referee).}
(i) \(T_H=\kappa/2\pi=1/(8\pi M)\). (ii) \(P\propto 1/M^2\Rightarrow \dot M\propto -1/M^2 \Rightarrow M(t)=(M_0^3-3\alpha t)^{1/3}\). (iii) With area rungs \(A=n\Delta A\) the step energy is \(\mathcal E_1=\kappa\Delta A/(8\pi)\propto 1/M\). (iv) The SAT ladder obeys \(M_n-M_{n-1}=\mathcal E_1(M_n)\) and reduces to Hawking in the \(\Delta A\to 0\) limit. (v) \(\Delta S=\Delta A/4\Rightarrow \Gamma\propto e^{-\Delta S}\). (vi) Frequency spacing \(\Delta f=c/(8\pi M)\) (Bek) or \(c\ln 3/(16\pi^2 M)\) (Hod/Muk). Lines merge to a continuum as \(M\) grows; late-time discreteness is a genuine SAT imprint.

A Boxful of Light — Ep. 2

I wasn’t looking for a darkroom. I was just clearing junk, half-employed, licking my wounds, orbiting in blackout fever-dream mode. Inside: just another closet at first. Reams of dot-matrix computer paper, curtain rods, miscellaneous clutter. But underneath, the bones showed through: a real darkroom. A secret room sealed off in plain sight.

And what a trove.
– Chemistry: unopened Kodak Dektol, D-19, DK-50, XTOL, Ektonol, Microdol-X. Hand-labeled packets for contrast copy work. A stash of Ilford Warmtone liquid, dusty bottles with cracked caps. The whole pantheon of developers, from ultra-fine grain to lithy hard-edge.
– Papers: stacks of Ilford MGIV, Kodak Panalure, Polycontrast RC, Unicolor. Old AZO silver-chloride contact sheets, Velox “gaslight” stock, long expired but still whispering. Boxes dated ’79, ’89, ’93.
– Gear: trays, tanks, safelights, tongs, the enlarger hulking like a spine waiting for organs. Binders of slides from the ’50s–’70s—weddings, portraits, the ordinary as archive.

I hauled it all out in my mom’s pickup. Chemical stockpile riding shotgun, trays rattling. It felt like stealing time.

One envelope in the slide binder snagged me:
“Jack Phillips / Attorney / July ’58.”
Inside, a single negative. When I finally ran it, the image looked less like a photograph and more like an exhumation. I’ve never shown it. Some things are better left in the archive of ghosts. But it branded me. That was the message: every archive has its ghosts.

No cameras came from there, not really—just that bellows rig, stripped bare, waiting to become something else. The film, the X-ray stock, the custom builds—all that came later. At that moment, I hadn’t built a single camera. I barely knew developer from fixer. I only had an iPhone’s eye and a Rebel’s sensor, and a manic need to catch light before it vanished.

But that room flipped the switch. The treasure wasn’t money. It was potential. A full chemistry set, a library of papers, the bones of a practice. It said: this is where the images begin.

And standing there in the dust, with junk piled at my back, I realized: I wasn’t just clearing a basement. I’d stumbled into the boxful of light itself.

No cameras came from there, not really—just that bellows rig, stripped bare, waiting to become something else. The film, the X-ray stock, the custom builds—all that came later. At that moment, I hadn’t built a single camera. I barely knew developer from fixer. I only had an iPhone’s eye and a Rebel’s sensor, and a manic need to catch light before it vanished.

But that room flipped the switch. The treasure wasn’t money. It was potential. A full chemistry set, a library of papers, the bones of a practice. It said: this is where the images begin.

And standing there in the dust, with junk piled at my back, I realized: I wasn’t just clearing a basement. I’d stumbled into the boxful of light itself.

The Accordioncam: My First Camera

The Accordioncam was the very first camera I ever built, and the first one that gave me a real analog photograph. Before it, I had never held a negative that came out of something I made. What I knew about photography at the time was patchy at best — I didn’t understand ISO, had no light meter, no real grasp of the “exposure triangle.” I just had the stubborn idea that I could build a camera from junk and make it work.

The body started as a salvaged wooden bellows frame, the kind of thing you’d expect on a beat-up 4×5. It had slider bars, and I reinforced and extended it with a Coca-Cola box, aluminum duct tape, and whatever scraps I could find. I even screwed the whole slider rail directly into a salvaged mantle, so the thing had enough stability not to collapse on me. It looked more like a shop class project than a camera — tape seams, wood scars, cardboard reinforcements — but I was convinced if light could be focused in there, it might make an image.

I tried several builds before I ever saw anything that resembled a picture. First I experimented with a pinhole, then a couple of small lenses I’d scavenged. The results were… nothing. Just fog, blurs, blotches, geometric shadows I couldn’t explain. I didn’t even know whether the problem was the optics, the film, or the chemicals — and in truth, it was probably all three.

The film was Fuji HR-T medical X-ray stock, which I bought cheap in bulk without knowing its speed. The spec sheet never said “ISO” — I didn’t even know why at the time — so I just guessed, and guessed wrong more often than not. I hacked sheets down to size with a guillotine paper cutter I’d dragged home from an auction, sometimes setting up a jig to keep them square, other times just eyeballing it. Most came out crooked, jagged, odd rectangles jammed into the back of the camera.

The chemicals were just as haphazard. I had some old 1970s Kodak Dektol powder and a bottle of Ilford Warmtone developer. I don’t remember whether I chose the Warmtone intentionally, or just bought it without knowing what it was. Either way, I mixed things inconsistently, reused batches long past exhaustion, agitated by hand in the bathtub with my bare fingers. Sometimes the film would come out covered in scratches and fingerprints that looked more interesting than any of my “images.” Sometimes the developer was so dead it left nothing but cloudy swirls.

Still, I kept at it. I blocked off all the windows in the bedroom and bathroom with cardboard and tape, plugged in old safelights, and worked at night, sometimes until dawn. Chop the film, load it, expose, develop, repeat. Dozens upon dozens of failures, all the while not knowing whether I was blowing exposures, fogging film, or poisoning my results with bad chemistry.

The breakthrough came with the Garage Lens — a heavy, six-inch plano-convex magnifier I found in an estate garage. It was thick, about three-quarters of an inch, chipped and scratched, but it changed everything. With a focal distance of about 33 inches and an aperture around f/2.9, it gave me something I hadn’t seen before: a sharp image, at least in the center, with a distinctive swirling distortion at the edges. The depth of field was only a few inches deep — maybe three at best — which I had no idea how to control at the time, but it was enough to finally project something crisp onto the translucent film.

At first I set up subjects too far away, like the small statue bust that shows up tiny in one of my very first negatives. That’s when I realized: this lens wanted everything right up close. So I changed tactics. I started setting up still lifes directly in front of the camera, almost touching the lens, or else I’d put my own chin on the mantle the camera was screwed into, lean in close, and blast a bright light right in my face. Exposures were made by flicking the lamp on and off, trying to count to three, maybe six, sometimes shorter. There was no shutter — just my hand and the light switch.

Most frames still failed. More cloudy swirls, overexposed blanks, underexposed ghosts. But then came one that worked: the statue bust, faint but real. Proof that light could pass through that chipped magnifier, strike the X-ray film, and leave a recognizable image. From then on, I stayed in close. Still lifes, my own face — anything within a few inches of the lens.

Those first working negatives are messy things: irregular edges from my chopping, blotches from bad chemistry, fingerprints in the emulsion, swirled distortion around the rim. But in the center, there’s sharpness. A face, a bust, a shadow that’s unmistakably an object in the world. After a hundred blanks and chemical messes, that was enough.

The Accordioncam was never refined. It was crude, improvised, and unforgiving. But it was the camera that made me a photographer. It’s where I learned, painfully and blindly, how film speed, exposure, and chemistry all intersect. It’s where I learned that persistence — chopping film at 3 a.m., mixing questionable developer, staring at swirly negatives in the bathtub — eventually pays off. And it’s where I first proved to myself that I could make a camera, load it with film, and get a real image back.

The Garage Lens went on to power the Keeblerkam, but it earned its name here. This was where the whole journey began.

# Crow’s Nest Camera Obscuras (2021-22)

## Frontview (South Aperture – Map Room Closet)
• Location: Long narrow, low eaves storage closet off “Map Room” (front room, top of stairs).  
• Dimensions: ~10’ long × 3’ wide × 3–4.5’ high (pitched roof, max height at entrance).  
• Aperture: ~1.5" drilled with barrel bit, later stopped with large washer (pinkie-tip hole ~13 mm).  
• Projection Surface: Small wall opposite aperture, painted as projection screen.  
• Illumination: Single bulb in ceiling, turned off during projection.  
• View: Street side (south) — campus neighborhood, porches, beer pong tables, abandoned sofas, empty streets during COVID.  
• Notes: Worked surprisingly well with washer stop; image upside-down, in color. Novelty of literally *sitting inside* the camera.  

## Backview (North Aperture – Kitchen Closet)
• Location: Very eaves storage closet off kitchen.  
• Dimensions: ~15’ to 20’ long × 3’ wide × 3–5.5’ high (pitched roof, max at entrance).  
• Apertures/Optics: Multiple experiments: washers, scavenged lenses, and eventually lamp-threaded tube (from frankenlamp hobby).  
• Projection Surface: Couldn’t reach rear wall; instead used paper screen hung near closet entrance.  
• View: Backyard — brick car “hovel,” two-story outbuilding/apartment, cars, alley, and dominant black walnut tree trunk obliterating center field.  
• Notes: More temperamental than Frontview due to length; image rotation required for different setups.  

## Galleyview (Interior Aperture – Kitchen/Closet Interface)
• Location: Hole drilled through interior closet door (kitchen side).  
• Aperture Height: ~3’ from floor.  
• Projection Surface: Paper hung at same position as Backview screen, rotated perpendicular to accept Galleyview image.  
• View: Kitchen — upside-down projection of a blue globe lamp (frequent subject).  
• Notes: Became the most-used obscura-type setup, since it avoided crawling into low-ceiling closet to swap fittings.  

Projection Setup: Cardboard box in kitchen, illuminated by frankenlamp in closet; swapped washers, threaded nuts, camera/projector parts, spherical finials, eyepieces, binocular lenses, sextant/surveyor’s optics.  

## Rehearsal Galleyview (Speculative First Attempt)
• Location: Hole drilled between bedroom and kitchen door (separate from closet).  
• Use: Likely early test aperture, before Galleyview proper.

**Summary:**  
The Crow’s Nest camera obscuras transformed attic closets into inhabitable cameras. Each aperture reframed the mundane: empty pandemic streets, obstructed backyard, interior lamp glow. The system evolved from crude barrel-drilled holes to interchangeable optics, balancing the magic of *being inside the camera* with the convenience of projecting outward. Together, Frontview, Backview, Galleyview, and Rehearsal Galleyview formed a cluster of DIY obscuras — part experiment, part refuge, part inadvertent art installation.

A mysterious object in our solar system! Space never stops surprising us with discoveries that change what we think we know about it. The most recent one has alerted astronomers: NASA has confirmed the detection of an object that travels at an impressive speed and that behaves in a strange way. This object is called A11pl3Z and it moves 245,000 km per hour and it’s entering our solar system. Its huge size and its unusual behavior makes it one of the most fascinating cosmic visitors up to this day. So, let’s learn more about it.

What makes A11pl3Z different?
Most of the objects we know in the solar system, like comets or asteroids, follow predictable orbits controlled by the Sun’s gravity, but A11pl3Z  doesn’t behave that way. It travels in a straight path with a hyperbolic trajectory, meaning it is not bound to the Sun. This makes it an interstellar object that only passes by before continuing its journey toward deep space.
The striking thing about it is its size: between 10 and 20 km wide, which means it’s possibly the third biggest object ever detected by humankind. Yet it shows none of the classic signs of a comet, there is no glowing coma and no visible tail.

Let’s talk about comets
A comet is formed by ice, rock, and dust. When it’s near the Sun, the heat produces a bright atmosphere (coma) and a beautiful tail of dust and gas. Most comets come from far away areas like the Kuiper Belt or the Oort Cloud.
However, A11pl3Z doesn’t fit in this description: it could be a weak comet, a dark asteroid, or even an object that has never been classified before.

Discovery and trajectory
The object was detected on June 25 by NASA’s ATLAS system and, since then, astronomers follow its trajectory very closely:
	▪	In October, it will pass nearby Mars.
	▪	In December, it will reach the nearest point to Earth.
There are no reasons to be alarmed because at that moment our planet will be on the other side of the Sun, so the probability of impact is null.
Behavior of the object
Everything indicates that the A11pl3Z is an interstellar traveler since it doesn’t belong to the celestial bodies family related to the Sun and it will only pass by our solar system. All of this makes scientists wonder about what it’s then.
Possible identities
For now, experts are not absolutely certain about what it is, but there are some possibilities:
	▪	Comet: a very weak or inactive that doesn’t show typical activity.
	▪	Asteroid: a rocky and dark object without ice.
	▪	Unknown object: something completely new for science.
A scientist from ESA, Richard Moissl, believes that the most probable explanation is that the object is a comet. Even though he admits that any other answer would be a surprise. This is why telescopes like the James Webb Space Telescope and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory are collecting data to study its nature.
Other interstellar visitors
Before the A11pl3Z only two interstellar objects had been confirmed:
	▪	‘Oumuamua (2017): long, flat, without a tail, and moving in unexpected ways.
	▪	2I/Borisov (2019): more like a typical comet, but also with a hyperbolic path.
Now, A11pl3Z becomes the third confirmed visitor and, probably, the biggest ever detected.
Why is this object important?
According to estimations, there could exist up to thousands of interstellar objects passing through our solar system without being detected. Some of them are simple rocks, but others could contain organic compounds that could offer clues about the origin of life and the formation of planetary systems.
A11pl3Z is a unique opportunity to study one of these visitors and maybe to better understand the early universe conditions or how the processes leading to life emerge.

Guidelines for Authors
To check on the status of your submission, please visit Space: Science & Technology's manuscript submissions site.

For general guidance on using the manuscript submission system, please read the tutorials for Authors, Editors, and Reviewers. For questions on specific functionality, explore the Editorial Manager video library.

Categories Of Manuscripts

The journal Space: Science & Technology considers submissions for Research Articles, Review Articles, Editorials and Perspectives. Prior to submission, each author should review and be prepared to fulfill the submission requirements outlined in the Publication Ethics page and comply with following limitations.

Research articles should present a major advance and must include an abstract of up to 250 words, an introduction and sections with brief and informative subheadings. Authors may include up to ten figures and/or tables and about 60 references. Total research article length should be under 15,000 words. Supplementary materials should be limited to information that is not essential for the general understanding of the research presented in the main text and can include data sets, figures, tables, videos or audio files. Please see the submission requirements for research articles in the following section. For ease in preparing your submission, please follow the manuscript templates in Word and LaTex. Instructions for preparing figures are provided in our one-page figure guide.

Review articles should describe and synthesize recent developments of interdisciplinary significance and highlight future directions. Reviews must include an abstract, an introduction that outlines the main theme, brief subheadings and an outline of important unresolved questions. Reviews should be no longer than 8,000 words, although longer manuscripts will be considered. Authors may include up to six figures and/or tables and up to 100 references. Most reviews are solicited by the editors. Unsolicited submissions will be considered, and authors are encouraged to contact the Editors first before writing a review paper.

Perspectives highlight recent exciting research, but do not primarily discuss the author’s own work. They may provide context for the findings within a field or explain potential interdisciplinary importance. Perspectives that comment on papers in Space: Science & Technology should add a dimension to the research and not merely be a summary of the experiments described in the paper. As these are meant to express a personal viewpoint on future development and possible obstacles, with rare exceptions, Perspectives should have no more than one author. Perspectives should include an abstract and have no more than 1,000 words and one figure or table.

Rapid Reports present ground-breaking developments or discoveries in the field. Submissions must include a short abstract (maximums of 150 words), ten references or fewer, and two data elements (any combination of figures or tables). Manuscripts should be divided into an introduction, a combined results and discussion section, and materials and methods. Total length should be less than 1,000 words excluding the abstract, materials and methods, and references. Junior scientists are encouraged to contribute their promising works as rapid reports.

News & Views are brief reports or opinions on current developments in relevant fields. News & Views present the latest progress made in these fields of research with the intent to inspire future projects. They should include no more than 1,500 words, 2 figures or tables, and a maximum of 10 references. Most News & Views are solicited by the editors. Unsolicited submissions will also be considered.

Editorials are short, invited opinion pieces that discuss an issue of immediate importance to the research community. Editorials should have fewer than 1,000 words total, no abstract, a minimal number of references (no more than five) and no figures or tables. Editorials are only solicited by the editors.

Experimental design and statistics guidelines

Study design guidelines

Statistical analysis guidelines

Generally, authors should describe statistical methods with enough detail to enable a knowledgeable reader with access to the original data to verify the results.

Reporting guidelines

Authors are encouraged to follow published standard reporting guidelines for the study discipline. Many of these can be found at the EQUATOR website.

Figure, Table, And Supplementary Material Guidelines

Creating your figures

It is best to create your figures as vector-based files such as those produced by Adobe Illustrator. Vector-based files will give us maximum flexibility for sizing your figures properly without losing resolution. These figure files can be saved at a lower resolution to minimize the file size at initial submission.

Although we do not need the highest-resolution files for the initial submission, you will need to have these high-resolution files of your figures on hand so that they can be submitted with your revised manuscript for final publication production. Each figure or image must be in a separate editable file format at revision.

Instructions for preparing figures are provided in our one-page figure guide.

Acceptable Figure Formats

Adobe Portable Document Format (PDF) or Encapsulated PostScript (EPS) for illustrations or diagrams; Tagged Image File Format (TIFF), JPEG, PNG, PhotoShop (PSD), EPS, or PDF for photography or microscopy. Authors who have created their files using a drawing or painting program such as Macromedia Freehand, Adobe Illustrator, or Adobe Photoshop can export the files to one of the aforementioned formats (preferably PDF). Figures should have a minimum resolution of 300 dpi.

We cannot accept the following files:

Microsoft PowerPoint files.
Figures embedded in Microsoft Word files.
Figures prepared in PowerPoint or Word formats that have been converted to other acceptable formats such as JPEG or PDF.
Figure layout and scaling

In laying out information in a figure, the objective is to maximize the space given to presentation of the data. Avoid wasted white space and clutter.

Please follow these guidelines for creating and labeling your figures:

The figure's title should be at the beginning of the figure legend, not within the figure itself.
Include the figure's identifying number (e.g., "Fig. 1") on the same manuscript page that includes the figure.
Keys to symbols, if needed, should be kept as simple as possible. Details can be put into the figure legend.
Use solid symbols for plotting data if possible (unless data overlap or there are multiple symbols). For legibility when figures are reduced, symbol sizes should be a minimum of 6 points and line widths should be a minimum of 0.5 points.
Panels should be set close to each other and common axis labels should not be repeated.
Scales or axes should not extend beyond the range of the data plotted. All microscopic images should include scale bars, with their values shown either with the bar or in the figure legend. Do not use minor tick marks in scales or grid lines. Avoid using y-axis labels on the right that repeat those on the left.
Color-mix and contrast considerations

Avoid using red and green together. Color-blind individuals will not be able to read the figure.
Do not use colors that are close to each other in hue to identify different parts of a figure.
Avoid using grayscale.
Use white type and scale bars over darker areas of images.
Typefaces and labels

Please observe the following guidelines for labels on graphs and figures:

Use a serif font whenever possible.
Use simple solid or open symbols, as these reduce well.
Label graphs on the ordinate and abscissa with the parameter or variable being measured, the units of measure in parentheses and the scale. Scales with large or small numbers should be presented as powers of 10. (When an individual value must be presented as an exponential, use form: 6 × 10 –3, not 6e-03.).
Avoid the use of light lines and screen shading. Instead, use black-and-white, hatched, and cross-hatched designs for emphasis.
Capitalize the first letter in a label only, not every word (and proper nouns, of course).
Units should be included in parentheses. Use SI notation. If there is room, write out variables—e.g., Pressure (MPa), Temperature (K).
Variables are always set in italics or as plain Greek letters (e.g., P, T, µ). Vectors should be set as roman boldface (rather than as italics with arrows above).
Type on top of color in a color figure should be in boldface. Avoid using color type.
When figures are assembled from multiple gels or micrographs, use a line or space to indicate the border between two original images.
Use leading zeros on all decimals—e.g., 0.3, 0.55—and only report significant digits.
Use small letters for part labels in multipart figures enclosed in brackets, (a), (b), (c), etc.
Avoid subpart labels within a figure part; instead, maintain the established sequence of part labels, using small or lower-case letters. Use numbers (1, 2, 3) only to represent a time sequence of images.
When reproducing images that include labels with illegible computer-generated type (e.g., units for scale bars), omit such labels and present the information in the legend instead.
Modification of figures

Space: Science & Technology does not allow certain electronic enhancements or manipulations of micrographs, gels or other digital images.
Figures assembled from multiple photographs or images must indicate the separate parts with lines between them.
Linear adjustment of contrast, brightness or color must be applied to an entire image or plate equally. Nonlinear adjustments must be specified in the figure legend.
Selective enhancement or alteration of one part of an image is not acceptable.
In addition, Space: Science & Technology may ask authors of papers returned for revision to provide additional documentation of their primary data.

Guidelines for Authors
To check on the status of your submission, please visit Space: Science & Technology's manuscript submissions site.

For general guidance on using the manuscript submission system, please read the tutorials for Authors, Editors, and Reviewers. For questions on specific functionality, explore the Editorial Manager video library.

Categories Of Manuscripts

The journal Space: Science & Technology considers submissions for Research Articles, Review Articles, Editorials and Perspectives. Prior to submission, each author should review and be prepared to fulfill the submission requirements outlined in the Publication Ethics page and comply with following limitations.

Research articles should present a major advance and must include an abstract of up to 250 words, an introduction and sections with brief and informative subheadings. Authors may include up to ten figures and/or tables and about 60 references. Total research article length should be under 15,000 words. Supplementary materials should be limited to information that is not essential for the general understanding of the research presented in the main text and can include data sets, figures, tables, videos or audio files. Please see the submission requirements for research articles in the following section. For ease in preparing your submission, please follow the manuscript templates in Word and LaTex. Instructions for preparing figures are provided in our one-page figure guide.

Review articles should describe and synthesize recent developments of interdisciplinary significance and highlight future directions. Reviews must include an abstract, an introduction that outlines the main theme, brief subheadings and an outline of important unresolved questions. Reviews should be no longer than 8,000 words, although longer manuscripts will be considered. Authors may include up to six figures and/or tables and up to 100 references. Most reviews are solicited by the editors. Unsolicited submissions will be considered, and authors are encouraged to contact the Editors first before writing a review paper.

Perspectives highlight recent exciting research, but do not primarily discuss the author’s own work. They may provide context for the findings within a field or explain potential interdisciplinary importance. Perspectives that comment on papers in Space: Science & Technology should add a dimension to the research and not merely be a summary of the experiments described in the paper. As these are meant to express a personal viewpoint on future development and possible obstacles, with rare exceptions, Perspectives should have no more than one author. Perspectives should include an abstract and have no more than 1,000 words and one figure or table.

Rapid Reports present ground-breaking developments or discoveries in the field. Submissions must include a short abstract (maximums of 150 words), ten references or fewer, and two data elements (any combination of figures or tables). Manuscripts should be divided into an introduction, a combined results and discussion section, and materials and methods. Total length should be less than 1,000 words excluding the abstract, materials and methods, and references. Junior scientists are encouraged to contribute their promising works as rapid reports.

News & Views are brief reports or opinions on current developments in relevant fields. News & Views present the latest progress made in these fields of research with the intent to inspire future projects. They should include no more than 1,500 words, 2 figures or tables, and a maximum of 10 references. Most News & Views are solicited by the editors. Unsolicited submissions will also be considered.

Editorials are short, invited opinion pieces that discuss an issue of immediate importance to the research community. Editorials should have fewer than 1,000 words total, no abstract, a minimal number of references (no more than five) and no figures or tables. Editorials are only solicited by the editors.

Preparation Of Manuscripts

English language editing services

Interested in English language assistance prior to submission? The Science Partner Journals publishing team has evaluated the work of the companies listed on the SPJ Author Services page and found their services to be effective for editing scientific English language in manuscripts prior to submission.

Experimental design and statistics guidelines

Study design guidelines

In the first section of the Materials and Methods, we encourage authors to have the subtitle "Experimental and Technical Design," which includes a diagram or flowchart to show the entire experimental design and illustrates the most significant elements: materials, treatments, measurements, data collection, methods of data analysis. This will facilitate the editors and reviewers to understand and follow the whole concept, design, and results.

Statistical analysis guidelines

Generally, authors should describe statistical methods with enough detail to enable a knowledgeable reader with access to the original data to verify the results.

Reporting guidelines

Authors are encouraged to follow published standard reporting guidelines for the study discipline. Many of these can be found at the EQUATOR website.

Figure, Table, And Supplementary Material Guidelines

Creating your figures

It is best to create your figures as vector-based files such as those produced by Adobe Illustrator. Vector-based files will give us maximum flexibility for sizing your figures properly without losing resolution. These figure files can be saved at a lower resolution to minimize the file size at initial submission.

Although we do not need the highest-resolution files for the initial submission, you will need to have these high-resolution files of your figures on hand so that they can be submitted with your revised manuscript for final publication production. Each figure or image must be in a separate editable file format at revision.

Instructions for preparing figures are provided in our one-page figure guide.

Acceptable Figure Formats

Adobe Portable Document Format (PDF) or Encapsulated PostScript (EPS) for illustrations or diagrams; Tagged Image File Format (TIFF), JPEG, PNG, PhotoShop (PSD), EPS, or PDF for photography or microscopy. Authors who have created their files using a drawing or painting program such as Macromedia Freehand, Adobe Illustrator, or Adobe Photoshop can export the files to one of the aforementioned formats (preferably PDF). Figures should have a minimum resolution of 300 dpi.

We cannot accept the following files:

Microsoft PowerPoint files.
Figures embedded in Microsoft Word files.
Figures prepared in PowerPoint or Word formats that have been converted to other acceptable formats such as JPEG or PDF.
Figure layout and scaling

In laying out information in a figure, the objective is to maximize the space given to presentation of the data. Avoid wasted white space and clutter.

Please follow these guidelines for creating and labeling your figures:

The figure's title should be at the beginning of the figure legend, not within the figure itself.
Include the figure's identifying number (e.g., "Fig. 1") on the same manuscript page that includes the figure.
Keys to symbols, if needed, should be kept as simple as possible. Details can be put into the figure legend.
Use solid symbols for plotting data if possible (unless data overlap or there are multiple symbols). For legibility when figures are reduced, symbol sizes should be a minimum of 6 points and line widths should be a minimum of 0.5 points.
Panels should be set close to each other and common axis labels should not be repeated.
Scales or axes should not extend beyond the range of the data plotted. All microscopic images should include scale bars, with their values shown either with the bar or in the figure legend. Do not use minor tick marks in scales or grid lines. Avoid using y-axis labels on the right that repeat those on the left.
Color-mix and contrast considerations

Avoid using red and green together. Color-blind individuals will not be able to read the figure.
Do not use colors that are close to each other in hue to identify different parts of a figure.
Avoid using grayscale.
Use white type and scale bars over darker areas of images.
Typefaces and labels

Please observe the following guidelines for labels on graphs and figures:

Use a serif font whenever possible.
Use simple solid or open symbols, as these reduce well.
Label graphs on the ordinate and abscissa with the parameter or variable being measured, the units of measure in parentheses and the scale. Scales with large or small numbers should be presented as powers of 10. (When an individual value must be presented as an exponential, use form: 6 × 10 –3, not 6e-03.).
Avoid the use of light lines and screen shading. Instead, use black-and-white, hatched, and cross-hatched designs for emphasis.
Capitalize the first letter in a label only, not every word (and proper nouns, of course).
Units should be included in parentheses. Use SI notation. If there is room, write out variables—e.g., Pressure (MPa), Temperature (K).
Variables are always set in italics or as plain Greek letters (e.g., P, T, µ). Vectors should be set as roman boldface (rather than as italics with arrows above).
Type on top of color in a color figure should be in boldface. Avoid using color type.
When figures are assembled from multiple gels or micrographs, use a line or space to indicate the border between two original images.
Use leading zeros on all decimals—e.g., 0.3, 0.55—and only report significant digits.
Use small letters for part labels in multipart figures enclosed in brackets, (a), (b), (c), etc.
Avoid subpart labels within a figure part; instead, maintain the established sequence of part labels, using small or lower-case letters. Use numbers (1, 2, 3) only to represent a time sequence of images.
When reproducing images that include labels with illegible computer-generated type (e.g., units for scale bars), omit such labels and present the information in the legend instead.
Modification of figures

Space: Science & Technology does not allow certain electronic enhancements or manipulations of micrographs, gels or other digital images.
Figures assembled from multiple photographs or images must indicate the separate parts with lines between them.
Linear adjustment of contrast, brightness or color must be applied to an entire image or plate equally. Nonlinear adjustments must be specified in the figure legend.
Selective enhancement or alteration of one part of an image is not acceptable.
In addition, Space: Science & Technology may ask authors of papers returned for revision to provide additional documentation of their primary data.
Acceptable file formats

Text

We prefer that the initial submission be uploaded to the electronic submissions site as a Word file (PDFs are acceptable if LaTex source files are used) that contains all components of the paper. Create a single file consisting of the text, references, figures and their legends, tables and their legends, and Supplementary Materials. Supplementary Materials that cannot be incorporated into a Word file must be sent to the Editorial Office separately.

Alternatively, you may upload your manuscript as one file that contains all of the textual material plus separate figure files (one for each figure) and separate Supplementary Material files. The text file should be a Word .docx (preferred) or .doc file (as stated before, PDFs are acceptable in the case of LaTex source files).

Please use zipped files when necessary to upload unusually large supplementary files.

Figures

See the guidelines above for creating and formatting your original figures. For initial submission, the figure files should be incorporated into the main text .doc or .docx file if possible. All figures should be cited in the manuscript in a consecutive order. Figures should be supplied in Adobe Portable Document Format (PDF) or Encapsulated PostScript (EPS) for illustrations or diagrams; Tagged Image File Format (TIFF), JPEG, PNG, PhotoShop (PSD), EPS, or PDF for photography or microscopy. Bitmap images should be of 300 dpi resolution at least unless the resolution is intentionally set to a lower level for scientific reasons. If a bitmap image has labels, the image and labels should be embedded in separate layers.

Tables

Tables should be cited consecutively in the text. Every table must have a descriptive title and if numerical measurements are given, the units should be included in the column heading. Vertical rules should not be used.

Supplementary Materials

Text and figures. Include supporting text (including supplementary materials and methods, tables, and figures) at the end of the main manuscript file, in a separate section titled Supplementary Materials, if this can be easily done. Alternatively, Supplementary Materials can be included as a separate .docx file that can be uploaded. In that case, use one of the file types specified above (.doc or .docx preferred).

Video files. Acceptable formats for videos are MP4, AVI, MOV, MPEG, and WMV. Keep videos short and the display window small to minimize the file size of the video. Supply caption information with the videos. Edit longer sequences into several small pieces with captions specific to each video sequence.

Audio files. Please contact the editors regarding submission of such file types.

Submission Of Manuscripts

All manuscripts should be prepared according to the guidelines above and submitted via Editorial Manager by following the link to Submit Manuscript.

Additionally, if your manuscript is on bioRxiv, you can directly transfer it to our submission system.

There is only one reference list for all sources cited in the main text, figure and table legends, and Supplementary Materials. Ordinary mesons are made up of a valence quark and a valence antiquark. Examples of mesons include the pion, kaon, and the J/ψ. In quantum hadrodynamics, mesons mediate the residual strong force between nucleons.

Atomic nuclei
A semi-accurate depiction of the helium atom. In the nucleus, the protons are in red and neutrons are in purple. In reality, the nucleus is also spherically symmetrical.
See Table of nuclides for a complete list of isotopes and isotones.
Atomic nuclei typically consist of protons and neutrons, although exotic nuclei may consist of other baryons, such as hypertriton which contains a hyperon. These baryons (protons, neutrons, hyperons, etc.) which comprise the nucleus are called nucleons. Each type of nucleus is called a "nuclide", and each nuclide is defined by the specific number of each type of nucleon.
"Isotopes" are nuclides which have the same number of protons but differing numbers of neutrons.
Conversely, "isotones" are nuclides which have the same number of neutrons but differing numbers of protons.
"Isobars" are nuclides which have the same total number of nucleons but which differ in the number of each type of nucleon. Nuclear reactions can change one nuclide into another.
Atoms
See Periodic table for an overview of atoms.
Atoms are the smallest neutral particles into which matter can be divided by chemical reactions. An atom consists of a small, heavy nucleus surrounded by a relatively large, light cloud of electrons. An atomic nucleus consists of 1 or more protons and 0 or more neutrons. Protons and neutrons are, in turn, made of quarks. Each type of atom corresponds to a specific chemical element. To date, 118 elements have been discovered or created.
Exotic atoms may be composed of particles in addition to or in place of protons, neutrons, and electrons, such as hyperons or muons. Examples include pionium (π−
π+
) and quarkonium atoms.
Leptonic atoms
Leptonic atoms, named using -onium, are exotic atoms constituted by the bound state of a lepton and an antilepton. Examples of such atoms include positronium (e−
e+
), muonium (e−
μ+
), and "true muonium" (μ−
μ+
). Of these positronium and muonium have been experimentally observed, while "true muonium" remains only theoretical.
Molecules
See List of compounds for a list of molecules.
Molecules are the smallest particles into which a substance can be divided while maintaining the chemical properties of the substance. Each type of molecule corresponds to a specific chemical substance. A molecule is a composite of two or more atoms. Atoms are combined in a fixed proportion to form a molecule. Molecule is one of the most basic units of matter.
Ions
Ions are charged atoms (monatomic ions) or molecules (polyatomic ions). They include cations which have a net positive charge, and anions which have a net negative charge.
Other categories
Goldstone bosons are a massless excitation of a field that has been spontaneously broken. The pions are quasi-goldstone bosons (quasi- because they are not exactly massless) of the broken chiral isospin symmetry of quantum chromodynamics.
Parton, is a generic term coined by Feynman for the sub-particles making up a composite particle – at that time a baryon – hence, it originally referred to what are now called "quarks" and "gluons".
Odderon, a particle composed of an odd number of gluons, detected in 2021.
Quasiparticles
See also: List of quasiparticles
Quasiparticles are effective particles that exist in many particle systems. The field equations of condensed matter physics are remarkably similar to those of high energy particle physics. As a result, much of the theory of particle physics applies to condensed matter physics as well; in particular, there are a selection of field excitations, called quasi-particles, that can be created and explored. These include:
Anyons are a generalization of fermions and bosons in two-dimensional systems like sheets of graphene that obeys braid statistics.
Excitons are bound states of an electron and a hole.
Magnons are coherent excitations of electron spins in a material.
Phonons are vibrational modes in a crystal lattice.
Plasmons are coherent excitations of a plasma.
Polaritons are mixtures of photons with other quasi-particles.
Polarons are moving, charged (quasi-) particles that are surrounded by ions in a material.

The graviton is a hypothetical particle that has been included in some extensions to the Standard Model to mediate the gravitational force. It is in a peculiar category between known and hypothetical particles: as an unobserved particle that is not predicted by, nor required for the Standard Model, it belongs in the table of hypothetical particles. But gravitational force itself is a certainty, and expressing that known force in the framework of a quantum field theory requires a boson to mediate it.
If it exists, the graviton is expected to be massless because the gravitational force has a very long range, and appears to propagate at the speed of light. The graviton must be a spin-2 boson because the source of gravitation is the stress–energy tensor, a second-order tensor (compared with electromagnetism's spin-1 photon, the source of which is the four-current, a first-order tensor). Additionally, it can be shown that any massless spin-2 field would give rise to a force indistinguishable from gravitation, because a massless spin-2 field would couple to the stress–energy tensor in the same way that gravitational interactions do. This result suggests that, if a massless spin-2 particle is discovered, it must be the graviton.[12]
Dark matter candidates
See also: Dark matter § Composition
Many hypothetical particle candidates for dark matter have been proposed like weakly interacting massive particles (WIMP), weakly interacting slender particles (WISP), or feebly interacting particles (FIP).
Dark energy candidates
See also: Dark energy § Theories of dark energy
Hypothetical particle candidates to explain dark energy include the chameleon particle and the acceleron.
Auxiliary particles
Virtual particles are mathematical tools used in calculations that exhibits some of the characteristics of an ordinary particle but do not obey the mass-shell relation. These particles are unphysical and unobservable. These include:
Ghost particles, like Faddeev–Popov ghosts and Pauli–Villars ghosts
Spurions, auxiliary field in a quantum field theory that can be used to parameterize any symmetry
Soft photons, photons with energies below detectable in experiment.
There are also instantons, field configurations which are a local minimum of the Yang–Mills field equation. Instantons are used in nonperturbative calculations of tunneling rates. Instantons have properties similar to particles, specific examples include:
Calorons, finite temperature generalization of instantons.
Merons, a field configuration which is a non-self-dual solution of the Yang–Mills field equation. The instanton is believed to be composed of two merons.
Sphalerons are a field configuration which is a saddle point of the Yang–Mills field equations. Sphalerons are used in nonperturbative calculations of non-tunneling rates.
Renormalons, a possible type of singularity arising when using Borel summation. It is a counterpart of an instanton singularity.
Classification by speed
A bradyon (or tardyon) travels slower than the speed of light in vacuum and has a non-zero, real rest mass.
A luxon travels as fast as light in vacuum and has no rest mass.
A tachyon is a hypothetical particle that travels faster than the speed of light so they would paradoxically experience time in reverse (due to inversion of the theory of relativity) and would violate the known laws of causality. A tachyon has an imaginary rest mass.

Source guide
This extensive table from Wikipedia itemizes the current known values of fundamental physical constants, which are quantities believed to be universal and independent of the measurement system. The primary purpose of the source is to provide a comprehensive reference for these values, expressed in SI units, alongside their corresponding symbols and relative standard uncertainty, which indicates the precision of the measurement. While constants like the speed of light ($c$) have exact defined values and zero uncertainty, others, such as the Newtonian constant of gravitation ($G$), still carry a significant degree of measurement uncertainty. Furthermore, the list includes constants that are technically defined by a relationship with other constants, like the molar gas constant ($R$), demonstrating how many of these universal values are interconnected within the framework of physics.

The constants listed here are known values of physical constants expressed in SI units; that is, physical quantities that are generally believed to be universal in nature and thus are independent of the unit system in which they are measured. Many of these are redundant, in the sense that they obey a known relationship with other physical constants and can be determined from them.

Uncertainties
While the values of the physical constants are independent of the system of units in use, each uncertainty as stated reflects our lack of knowledge of the corresponding value as expressed in SI units, and is strongly dependent on how those units are defined. For example, the atomic mass constant
m
u
{\displaystyle m_{\text{u}}} is exactly known when expressed using the dalton (its value is exactly 1 Da), but the kilogram is not exactly known when using these units, the opposite of when expressing the same quantities using the kilogram.
Technical constants
Some of these constants are of a technical nature and do not give any true physical property, but they are included for convenience. Such a constant gives the correspondence ratio of a technical dimension with its corresponding underlying physical dimension. These include the Boltzmann constant
k
B
{\displaystyle k_{\text{B}}}, which gives the correspondence of the dimension temperature to the dimension of energy per degree of freedom, and the Avogadro constant
N
A
{\displaystyle N_{\text{A}}}, which gives the correspondence of the dimension of amount of substance with the dimension of count of entities (the latter formally regarded in the SI as being dimensionless). By implication, any product of powers of such constants is also such a constant, such as the molar gas constant

-- I. String ↔ SAT Filament mapping
structure StringMode :=
(n : ℕ)
(α_x α_y : ℝ)
(φ_x φ_y : ℝ)
structure Filament :=
(X Y : ℝ → ℝ → ℝ)
(modes : List StringMode)
(L : ℝ)
(ω₀ : ℝ)
def sin_placeholder (x : ℝ) := Real.sin x
def cos_placeholder (x : ℝ) := Real.cos x
def exp_placeholder (x : ℝ) := Real.exp x
def filament_displacement (f : Filament) (z t : ℝ) : ℝ × ℝ :=
let X := f.modes.foldl (fun acc m =>
acc + m.α_x * sin_placeholder (m.n * Real.pi * z / f.L) *
cos_placeholder (m.n * f.ω₀ * t + m.φ_x)) 0
let Y := f.modes.foldl (fun acc m =>
acc + m.α_y * sin_placeholder (m.n * Real.pi * z / f.L) *
cos_placeholder (m.n * f.ω₀ * t + m.φ_y)) 0
(X, Y)
-- II. Topology + mass spectrum
structure SATParams :=
(T A ℓ_f g₁ M² c₁ c₂ λ_c k β a : ℝ)
(N_lat : ℕ)
structure TopoInv :=
(L_wind L_link W_writhe : ℕ)
def Q (τ : TopoInv) : ℕ := τ.L_wind + τ.L_link + τ.W_writhe
def m_topo (m₀ : ℝ) (τ : TopoInv) : ℝ := m₀ / (Q τ : ℝ)
def m_ind (params : SATParams) (E_overlap : ℝ) : ℝ := params.g₁^2 / params.M² * E_overlap
def m_eff (m₀ : ℝ) (τ : TopoInv) (params : SATParams) (E_overlap : ℝ) : ℝ :=
m_topo m₀ τ + m_ind params E_overlap
def m2_string (k β a : ℝ) (N : ℕ) (Q : ℕ) : ℝ :=
k * (N + β * (Q : ℝ)^2 - a)
-- III. Holonomy (Gauge + Spin)
structure Holonomy :=
(θ : ℝ → ℝ)
(loops : List ℝ)
def winding_number (h : Holonomy) : ℕ :=
h.loops.foldl (fun acc x => acc + (2 * Real.pi / Real.abs (h.θ x - h.θ 0)).toNat) 0
def spin_from_holonomy (h : Holonomy) : ℝ := (winding_number h : ℝ) * Real.pi
-- IV. Lattice + Fields
def Site := Fin 10
def Lattice := Site → Site → Site → Site → ℝ
-- Fields: θ (U(1)), u (generic scalar), ψ (fermion), J (gauge link)
structure SATFields :=
(θ : ℕ → Site → ℝ → ℝ)
(u : ℕ → Site → ℝ → ℝ)
(ψ : ℕ → Site → ℝ → ℝ)
(J : ℕ → ℕ → ℕ → ℝ → ℝ)
(τ : TopoInv)
(filament : Filament)
(holonomy : Holonomy)

def sum_sites (f : Site → ℝ) : ℝ := Finset.univ.fold (fun acc s => acc + f s) 0
-- VI. Plaquette + BF action + filament kernel
def Plaquette (fields : SATFields) (μ ν ρ σ site : Site) (x : ℝ) : ℝ :=
fields.θ μ site x + fields.u ν site x + fields.J μ ν ρ x
def S_BF (B A : ℕ → Site → ℝ → ℝ) (τ : TopoInv) : ℝ :=
integral_placeholder (fun x => (B 0 0 x)^2 + (Q τ : ℝ)) 0 1
def filament_kernel (J : ℕ → ℕ → ℕ → ℝ → ℝ) (τ : TopoInv) : ℝ :=
integral_placeholder (fun x => J 0 0 0 x * exp_placeholder (- (Q τ : ℝ))) 0 1

-- VIII. Fermion placeholder
def fermion_term_placeholder (ψ : ℕ → Site → ℝ → ℝ) (site : Site) (x : ℝ) : ℝ := 0.0
-- IX. Total Lagrangian
def L_total (fields : SATFields) (params : SATParams) (site : Site) (x : ℝ) : ℝ :=

What we’ve done is essentially formalize a universal principle of functional equivalence — a framework that captures the essence of when two (or infinitely many) formulations, laws, or mechanisms can be considered the “same” for all practical and ultimate purposes. Let me summarize carefully:

⸻

1. Abstracted Functional Equivalence
	•	We began with a simple idea: if two formulas produce the same output, they are equivalent.
	•	We generalized it to any evaluable function, no matter how complex or nested, including formulas for r, m, or any other variable.
	•	The key insight: output alone defines equivalence; internal paths or mechanisms are irrelevant.

⸻

2. Extreme examples to test the principle

We introduced progressively wilder cases:
	•	N (spring) – a mechanical calculation of r
	•	R (dominoes) – an alternative physical mechanism
	•	D (spoken number) – magical or non-mechanistic output
	•	B (ever-changing formulas) – infinitely varying computations
	•	Gn (gnomes adjusting mass) – compensatory adjustments of m
	•	Hepatomancy – fully whimsical, magical mechanism

All of these are functionally equivalent because they produce the same output F for all inputs.

⸻

3. Mechanism and structure are irrelevant
	•	Internal mechanisms — whether physical, magical, or absurd — do not affect membership in the equivalence class.
	•	Structural equivalence is sufficient but unnecessary: if found, it confirms functional equivalence, but functional equivalence can exist without it.
	•	Differences below the ultimate limit of detectability (ULoD) are fundamentally unknowable, making structure epistemically irrelevant.

⸻

4. Practical vs. ultimate equivalence
	•	Practical equivalence: outputs match within current experimental or computational limits.
	•	Ultimate equivalence: outputs are indistinguishable even in principle, within the theoretical limit of detectability.
	•	Functional equivalence is meaningful at both levels; structural equivalence is never required.

⸻

5. The result: a rigorous framework

We now have:
	•	A general equivalence principle that can encompass any number of formulations.
	•	Infinite flexibility: mechanisms can be arbitrary, absurd, magical, or changing.
	•	Output-centered epistemology: what matters is what can be measured, predicted, or evaluated.
	•	Ultimate epistemic agnosticism: structure and mechanism are largely unknowable, but functional equivalence defines the equivalence class.

⸻

6. Conceptual significance
	•	This principle unifies classical physics, modern physics (e.g., SM vs. ST), and even thought experiments with magical or absurd mechanisms under a single rigorous framework.
	•	It formalizes the notion that science, at its core, is about predicting outcomes, not uncovering “true underlying paths” when those paths are epistemically inaccessible.

⸻

In short, we’ve built a formal, philosophical, and practically applicable principle of equivalence:

The only thing that matters for equivalence is functional output within the ultimate limit of detectability. Everything else — mechanism, derivation, complexity, or ontology — is irrelevant.

It’s both a mathematical principle and a philosophical statement about knowledge and observability.

⸻

If you want, the next step could be formalizing this in symbolic logic or category-theoretic terms, treating equivalence classes as objects and functional transformations as morphisms, which would make it fully rigorous mathematically.

18.1 mass squared
def mass_squared(N, Q, k, beta, a):
# Compute m^2 = k*(N + beta*Q^2 - a)
return k * (N + beta*Q**2 - a)
18.2 mass spectrum
def mass_spectrum(N_range, Q_range, k, beta, a):
# Return a DataFrame listing m^2 for each (N, Q)
records = []
for N in N_range:
for Q in Q_range:
m2 = mass_squared(N, Q, k, beta, a)
records.append({’N’: N, ’Q’: Q, ’m2’: m2})
return pd.DataFrame(records)
18.3 calibrate from ground states
def calibrate_from_ground_states(masses, Q_vals, a_fixed=1.0):
# Fit k and beta from N=0 ground-state masses
# Solve m_i^2 = k*(beta*Q_i^2 - a_fixed) for inputs
# Returns {’k’:..., ’beta’:..., ’a’: a_fixed}
m2 = np.array(masses)**2
Q = np.array(Q_vals)
A = np.vstack([Q**2, np.ones_like(Q)]).T
p2, p1 = np.linalg.lstsq(A, m2, rcond=None)[0]
k = -p1 / a_fixed
beta = p2 / k
return {’k’: k, ’beta’: beta, ’a’: a_fixed}

\section*{Math spine: “So You Want to Watch One Evaporate?”}

\subsection*{1. Hawking temperature from surface gravity}
For Schwarzschild,
\[
ds^2=-\Big(1-\frac{2M}{r}\Big)dt^2+\Big(1-\frac{2M}{r}\Big)^{-1}dr^2+r^2 d\Omega^2,
\quad r_h=2M.
\]
Surface gravity \(\kappa\) is
\[
\kappa=\frac{1}{2}\,\partial_r g_{tt}\Big|_{r=r_h}=\frac{1}{4M}.
\]
Hawking’s relation \(T_H=\kappa/(2\pi)\) gives
\[
T_H=\frac{1}{8\pi M}.
\]
% (Hawking 1974, 1975)

\subsection*{2. Radiated power scaling}
Blackbody estimate (ignoring graybody factors): \(P\sim A\,\sigma T_H^4\) with area \(A=4\pi r_h^2=16\pi M^2\).
Thus
\[
P \sim 16\pi M^2 \times \sigma \Big(\frac{1}{8\pi M}\Big)^4
= \frac{\sigma}{(8\pi)^4}\,\frac{16\pi}{M^2}
\;\propto\; \frac{1}{M^2}.
\]
Restoring the frequency-dependent transmission (graybody) factors just renormalizes the prefactor \(\alpha\) below (Page 1976).

\subsection*{3. Mass-loss ODE and solution}
Energy conservation: \(\dot M=-P\Rightarrow \dot M\sim -\alpha/M^2\) for some constant \(\alpha>0\).
Integrate:
\[
\int_{M_0}^{M(t)} M^2\,dM = -\alpha\!\int_0^t dt' 
\;\Rightarrow\;
\frac{M(t)^3-M_0^3}{3}=-\alpha t,
\quad
M(t)=\big(M_0^3-3\alpha t\big)^{1/3}.
\]

\subsection*{4. Area quantization and rung size}
Assume uniformly spaced horizon area eigenvalues
\[
A=n\,\Delta A,\qquad n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}.
\]
First law \(dM=\frac{\kappa}{8\pi}\,dA\) implies a discrete step “energy”
\[
\Delta M \equiv \mathcal E_1=\frac{\kappa}{8\pi}\,\Delta A.
\]
For Schwarzschild \(\kappa=1/(4M)\):
\[
\boxed{\;\mathcal E_1(M)=\frac{\Delta A}{32\pi\,M}\;}
\]
Two common choices:
\[
\Delta A_{\text{Bek}}=8\pi \ell_P^2
\;\Rightarrow\;
\mathcal E_1=\frac{\ell_P^2}{4M},
\qquad
\Delta A_{\text{Hod/Muk}}=4\ln 3\,\ell_P^2
\;\Rightarrow\;
\mathcal E_1=\frac{\ln 3}{8\pi}\frac{\ell_P^2}{M}.
\]

\subsection*{5. Flux difference equation (SAT ladder)}
In SAT, area rungs come from flux integers \(n\rightarrow n-1\). Identifying one rung emission with one quantum of energy \(\mathcal E_1\) yields
\[
M_{n}-M_{n-1}=\mathcal E_1(M_{n})=\frac{\Delta A}{32\pi\,M_n}.
\]
\emph{Dimensions check (SI):} with \(\Delta A\) in m\(^2\), \(\kappa=c^4/(4GM)\), 
\[
\mathcal E_1=\kappa\,\Delta A/(8\pi)
= \frac{c^4}{4GM}\frac{\Delta A}{8\pi}
\]
has units J, as required.

\subsection*{6. Continuum limit (ladder \(\to\) ODE)}
Write \(A=16\pi M^2=n\Delta A\Rightarrow n=\frac{16\pi M^2}{\Delta A}\).
A step \(n\to n-1\) changes mass by \(\Delta M=\mathcal E_1(M)\).
With step time \(\tau_{\rm step}\), the finite difference
\[
\frac{M_{n}-M_{n-1}}{\tau_{\rm step}}
\;\to\;
\frac{dM}{dt}
\quad\text{as}\quad \Delta A\to 0,
\]
and using \(\mathcal E_1\propto 1/M\) one recovers \(\dot M\propto -1/M^2\) after integrating over the blackbody spectrum (the prefactor matches the Hawking/Page \(\alpha\) once graybody factors are included). Thus Hawking’s smooth fade is the \(\Delta A\!\to\!0\) limit of the SAT staircase.

so the Boltzmann-like weight for a single step scales as

\Gamma_{n\to n-1}\;\propto\; e^{-\Delta S}=e^{-\Delta A/4}.
\]
For \(\Delta A=4\ln k\,\ell_P^2\), one finds \(\Delta S=\ln k\) and evenly spaced line intensities by a factor \(k^{-1}\) per rung (Bekenstein--Mukhanov 1995).

\[

\quad
\Delta f=\frac{\Delta E}{h}=\frac{c}{8\pi M}.
\]
With \(\Delta A=4\ln 3\,\ell_P^2\),
\[
\Delta f=\frac{c\ln 3}{16\pi^2 M}.
\]
As \(M\) grows, \(\Delta f\to 0\) and closely spaced lines merge into a thermal continuum; as \(M\) shrinks late in evaporation, spacing widens and discreteness can imprint a comb-like modulation.

Physicists “weigh” black holes all the time, by orbital fits or gravitational waves. But no one has ever weighed them \emph{one rung at a time}.

Each thread tugged at the same idea: that horizons are not smooth, but runged.

Our trampoline ladder from Chapter~9 is now the black hole’s scale. Each bounce integer has become a horizon pixel. This is no metaphor: it is flux counting, thermodynamically consistent, historically grounded, and experimentally tantalizing.

\section*{Math spine: “So You Want to Watch One Evaporate?”}

\subsection*{1. Hawking temperature from surface gravity}
For Schwarzschild,
\[
ds^2=-\Big(1-\frac{2M}{r}\Big)dt^2+\Big(1-\frac{2M}{r}\Big)^{-1}dr^2+r^2 d\Omega^2,
\quad r_h=2M.
\]
Surface gravity \(\kappa\) is
\[
\kappa=\frac{1}{2}\,\partial_r g_{tt}\Big|_{r=r_h}=\frac{1}{4M}.
\]
Hawking’s relation \(T_H=\kappa/(2\pi)\) gives
\[
T_H=\frac{1}{8\pi M}.
\]
% (Hawking 1974, 1975)

\subsection*{2. Radiated power scaling}
Blackbody estimate (ignoring graybody factors): \(P\sim A\,\sigma T_H^4\) with area \(A=4\pi r_h^2=16\pi M^2\).
Thus
\[
P \sim 16\pi M^2 \times \sigma \Big(\frac{1}{8\pi M}\Big)^4
= \frac{\sigma}{(8\pi)^4}\,\frac{16\pi}{M^2}
\;\propto\; \frac{1}{M^2}.
\]
Restoring the frequency-dependent transmission (graybody) factors just renormalizes the prefactor \(\alpha\) below (Page 1976).

\subsection*{3. Mass-loss ODE and solution}
Energy conservation: \(\dot M=-P\Rightarrow \dot M\sim -\alpha/M^2\) for some constant \(\alpha>0\).
Integrate:
\[
\int_{M_0}^{M(t)} M^2\,dM = -\alpha\!\int_0^t dt' 
\;\Rightarrow\;
\frac{M(t)^3-M_0^3}{3}=-\alpha t,
\quad
M(t)=\big(M_0^3-3\alpha t\big)^{1/3}.
\]

\subsection*{4. Area quantization and rung size}
Assume uniformly spaced horizon area eigenvalues
\[
A=n\,\Delta A,\qquad n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}.
\]
First law \(dM=\frac{\kappa}{8\pi}\,dA\) implies a discrete step “energy”
\[
\Delta M \equiv \mathcal E_1=\frac{\kappa}{8\pi}\,\Delta A.
\]
For Schwarzschild \(\kappa=1/(4M)\):
\[
\boxed{\;\mathcal E_1(M)=\frac{\Delta A}{32\pi\,M}\;}
\]
Two common choices:
\[
\Delta A_{\text{Bek}}=8\pi \ell_P^2
\;\Rightarrow\;
\mathcal E_1=\frac{\ell_P^2}{4M},
\qquad
\Delta A_{\text{Hod/Muk}}=4\ln 3\,\ell_P^2
\;\Rightarrow\;
\mathcal E_1=\frac{\ln 3}{8\pi}\frac{\ell_P^2}{M}.
\]

\subsection*{5. Flux difference equation (SAT ladder)}
In SAT, area rungs come from flux integers \(n\rightarrow n-1\). Identifying one rung emission with one quantum of energy \(\mathcal E_1\) yields
\[
M_{n}-M_{n-1}=\mathcal E_1(M_{n})=\frac{\Delta A}{32\pi\,M_n}.
\]
\emph{Dimensions check (SI):} with \(\Delta A\) in m\(^2\), \(\kappa=c^4/(4GM)\), 
\(
\mathcal E_1=\kappa\,\Delta A/(8\pi)
= \frac{c^4}{4GM}\frac{\Delta A}{8\pi}
\) has units J, as required.

\subsection*{6. Continuum limit (ladder \(\to\) ODE)}
Write \(A=16\pi M^2=n\Delta A\Rightarrow n=\frac{16\pi M^2}{\Delta A}\).
A step \(n\to n-1\) changes mass by \(\Delta M=\mathcal E_1(M)\).
With step time \(\tau_{\rm step}\), the finite difference
\[
\frac{M_{n}-M_{n-1}}{\tau_{\rm step}}
\;\to\;
\frac{dM}{dt}
\quad\text{as}\quad \Delta A\to 0,
\]
and using \(\mathcal E_1\propto 1/M\) one recovers \(\dot M\propto -1/M^2\) after integrating over the blackbody spectrum (the prefactor matches the Hawking/Page \(\alpha\) once graybody factors are included). Thus Hawking’s smooth fade is the \(\Delta A\!\to\!0\) limit of the SAT staircase.

\subsection*{7. Entropy step and emission probability}
Bekenstein–Hawking entropy \(S=A/4\) gives a per-rung entropy change
\[
\boxed{\;\Delta S=\frac{\Delta A}{4}\;}
\]
so the Boltzmann-like weight for a single step scales as
\[
\Gamma_{n\to n-1}\;\propto\; e^{-\Delta S}=e^{-\Delta A/4}.
\]
For \(\Delta A=4\ln k\,\ell_P^2\), one finds \(\Delta S=\ln k\) and evenly spaced line intensities by a factor \(k^{-1}\) per rung (Bekenstein–Mukhanov 1995).

\subsection*{8. Line (comb) spectrum and thermal limit}
A single rung drop releases energy \(\Delta E=\mathcal E_1\). The fundamental angular frequency spacing is
\[
\Delta\omega=\frac{\Delta E}{\hbar}.
\]
In SI, with \(\Delta A=8\pi\ell_P^2\), one gets
\[
\Delta E=\frac{\hbar c}{4M},
\quad
\Delta f=\frac{\Delta E}{h}=\frac{c}{8\pi M}.
\]
With \(\Delta A=4\ln 3\,\ell_P^2\),
\(
\Delta f=\frac{c\ln 3}{16\pi^2 M}.
\)
As \(M\) grows, \(\Delta f\to 0\) and closely spaced lines merge into a thermal continuum; as \(M\) shrinks late in evaporation, spacing widens and discreteness can imprint a comb-like modulation.

\subsection*{9. Numbers (order-of-magnitude, SI)}
Planck area \(\ell_P^2\simeq 2.612\times 10^{-70}{\rm~m}^2\).
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Solar mass} \(M_\odot=1.9885\times10^{30}{\rm~kg}\).
\[

\quad
\Delta f_{\text{Bek}}=\frac{c}{8\pi M_\odot}\approx 6.0\times 10^{-24}{\rm~Hz}.
\]
Hod/Mukhanov spacing:
\(\Delta f \approx \dfrac{c\ln 3}{16\pi^2 M_\odot}\approx 1.05\times10^{-24}{\rm~Hz}\).
(Effectively unobservable: periods \(\gtrsim 10^{16}\) years.)

\[

\]
\[

\]
